Czech Republic · A family archive story

Two days in Prague

We arrived from Dresden with a weekend, a love of old cities and a firm belief that breakfast and beer both deserved proper attention.

2 daysCity & cultureFood-led
Getting thereOld Town & lunchMala StranaDay twoWhat we learned

Prague had lived in our imagination as a city of medieval spires, cobbled lanes and old pubs. The reality was busier and more touristy than that romantic picture — but it was also full of moments that made us slow down: a quiet side street beyond the square, the first crackle of roasted pork skin, and a café where one pastry became the memory we still talk about.

The city worked best for us when we stopped treating the famous sights as a checklist and let food, trams and side streets shape the day.

Arriving from Dresden

We took a Eurolines bus from Dresden. Two comfortable hours later it dropped us at Florenc, directly beside the metro. That simple arrival shaped our first impression: Prague was easy to enter without a car, easy to navigate and compact enough that we could spend most of the weekend on foot.

Good to know

Stay within walking distance of the Old Town rather than beside every attraction. Prague’s centre rewards early mornings and late evenings, once the largest tour groups have moved on.

Old stones, Czech beer and an intimidating lunch

Our first glimpse of the Old Town Square came with market smoke in the air and the dark towers of the Týn church above the roofs. We were hungry, so our cultural education began at the table.

At U Tří Růží we ordered the roasted pork knuckle: crisp skin around tender meat, served with sauerkraut, bread, pickles and mustard. It was rich, excessive and completely right for the place. The brewery’s lighter lager was the sensible counterweight.

Worth the detour

Go hungry and share. Traditional Czech food is generous, meat-heavy and far more enjoyable when the meal is allowed to become part of the afternoon rather than a rushed stop between sights.

Across Charles Bridge to Mala Strana

Charles Bridge was crowded, but the views back across the river explained why everyone was there. The better discovery came after crossing it: Mala Strana’s quieter lanes, old façades and the sense that Prague had exhaled.

We chose Café Savoy because we had seen it on Anthony Bourdain’s No Reservations. Its restored interiors were beautiful, but this striped chocolate-and-orange pastry is what survived in our memory. It is a good example of why food belongs inside the story of a place rather than on a separate restaurant list.

A view from the top

On our second day we climbed the Astronomical Clock tower. The hourly spectacle below attracts a crowd, but the view above it was the real reward: red roofs, church spires and a city that suddenly made geographical sense.

We finished at Pivovarský Klub, an unassuming place with an enormous beer list. It was less photogenic than the square and more representative of the kind of travel moment we enjoy: a specific local obsession, discovered with enough time to sit and understand it.

What stayed with us

Prague was not an undiscovered city, and pretending otherwise would miss the point. What stayed with us was how easy it was to create a personal version of a famous place: walk early, stay out after dark, cross the river, use the tram and let a meal interrupt the plan.

We would do this differently

We would plan fewer major sights and reserve more time for neighbourhood wandering. Two days covers the landmarks; a third would make the experience feel less compressed.

Useful for another traveller

Late spring gave us comfortable walking weather without summer heat. Carry some Czech koruna, use public transport rather than a sightseeing bus and treat one historic café as part of the cultural itinerary.
